title: SQL Fundamentals
subtitle: Weeks 5-7: query any relational database
description: Build SQL from the ground up on a realistic sample database: selecting and filtering rows, NULLs, sorting, aggregates, joining tables, subqueries, and an introduction to CTEs and window functions. Most lessons have runnable queries.

lessons.title: Tables, Rows and Columns
lessons.body:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you ask a relational database a question. Data is stored in **tables**: a named grid with **columns** down the side and one **row** per thing. This course uses one realistic sample database throughout so you can build a mental model and keep reusing it:

| table | one row is... | columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `customers` | one customer account | id, name, plan, region |
| `orders` | one customer order | id, customer_id, status, total, ordered_on |
| `agents` | one support engineer | id, name, team, level |
| `tickets` | one support ticket | id, subject, status, priority, customer_id, agent_id, resolved_minutes |

Every query that reads data has the same skeleton: `SELECT` names the columns you want, and `FROM` names the table that holds them.

```sql
SELECT * FROM agents;
```

The `*` is shorthand for 'every column'. Read the query aloud: select all columns from the agents table. The result is a fresh grid; it never changes the stored data.

When you only need a few columns, list them, and the order you write them is the order they come back:

```sql
SELECT name, region FROM customers;
```

One column appears per name in your list, and one row per row of the table (until you start filtering). On its own, `SELECT` never removes duplicate rows or reorders them — those are separate jobs for later clauses. The **result shape** — its columns and row count — is the first thing to check whenever a query surprises you.

exercises.prompt: Show every column of every agent.
exercises.hint: The star stands for all columns.
exercises.explain: The star returns every column of every row - the whole agents table.

exercises.prompt: Show each customer's name and region, name first.
exercises.hint: List the two column names after SELECT, separated by a comma.
exercises.explain: You get exactly the columns you asked for, in the order you wrote them.

exercises.prompt: In the `orders` table, what does one row represent?
options: One customer order and its details
One column of the table
One customer's entire set of orders
The whole database
exercises.explain: One row per order. Each column (status, total, ordered_on...) is a property of that single order.
exercises.hint: Think about the noun the table is named after.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword names the table that a SELECT reads from?
exercises.hint: It is the second word of every read query in this course.
exercises.explain: SELECT names the columns; FROM names the table that holds them.

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE

exercises.prompt: List the subject and priority of every P1 ticket.
exercises.starter: SELECT subject, priority FROM tickets WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, priority FROM tickets WHERE priority = 'P1'
exercises.hint: P1 is text, so wrap it in single quotes.
exercises.explain: Three tickets carry P1: ids 1, 6 and 9.

exercises.prompt: List the subject and status of Open tickets that are also P1.
exercises.starter: SELECT subject, status FROM tickets WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, status FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open' AND priority = 'P1'
exercises.hint: Join the two conditions with AND.
exercises.explain: AND keeps only rows where both conditions hold: tickets 1 and 9.

exercises.prompt: List the id and total of every order worth more than 1000.
exercises.starter: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE
exercises.solution: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE total > 1000
exercises.hint: 1000 is a number, so no quotes are needed.
exercises.explain: Orders 1, 5 and 10 exceed 1000; the rest are 950 or below.

exercises.prompt: List the id of every order that is Paid or Pending and worth more than 1000.
exercises.solution: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE (status = 'Paid' OR status = 'Pending') AND total > 1000
exercises.hint: Wrap the two statuses in parentheses so AND applies to the whole group.
exercises.explain: Parentheses make OR bind first: only Paid/Pending orders above 1000 survive - 1, 5 and 10. Without them, every Paid order would pass.

lessons.title: Sorting and Limiting
lessons.body:
Rows come back in no guaranteed order. If order matters, ask for it with `ORDER BY`, and cut the list down with `LIMIT`:

```sql
SELECT id, subject FROM tickets ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3;
```

`ORDER BY` names the column to sort on. `ASC` is ascending (smallest first) and is the default; `DESC` is descending (largest first). Ticket ids grow over time, so `ORDER BY id DESC` puts the newest tickets first — a queue an agent can work straight down.

`LIMIT` keeps only the first N rows of whatever has been produced. Sorting happens **before** trimming, so the two clauses together answer everyday questions: the three newest tickets, the slowest resolutions, the largest orders.

The clauses have a fixed order, and writing them out of sequence is an error:

```
FROM  ->  WHERE  ->  ORDER BY  ->  LIMIT
```

So a filtered, sorted, capped query reads like this:

```sql
SELECT subject, resolved_minutes FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Resolved' ORDER BY resolved_minutes DESC LIMIT 1;
```

That returns the single slowest resolution. Swap `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` and the database refuses the query rather than guessing what you meant. Remember too that `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` trims an arbitrary set of rows, so pair them when the 'first N' really should mean something.

exercises.prompt: Show the three newest tickets: their id and subject, newest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, subject FROM tickets ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3
exercises.hint: Sort on id descending, then trim with LIMIT 3.
exercises.explain: Ids grow over time, so the highest ids are the newest tickets.

exercises.prompt: Among Resolved tickets, show the subject and resolved_minutes of all of them, slowest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT subject, resolved_minutes FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Resolved' ORDER BY resolved_minutes DESC
exercises.hint: Filter to Resolved so every row has a number, then sort the minutes descending.
exercises.explain: Descending puts the biggest number - the slowest fix - on top.

exercises.prompt: Show the id and total of the two largest orders, biggest first.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, total FROM orders ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 2
exercises.hint: ORDER BY total DESC, then keep only the first two rows.
exercises.explain: The two biggest totals are 2100 (order 5) and 1500 (order 10).

exercises.prompt: A query runs in a fixed order. Put these steps in the sequence the database follows.
items: Read the table named in FROM
Keep only matching rows with WHERE
Sort the surviving rows with ORDER BY
Trim the list to the first N rows with LIMIT
exercises.explain: FROM, then WHERE, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT - which is why you cannot write LIMIT before ORDER BY.
exercises.hint: Start with where the data comes from, finish with how much of it you keep.

lessons.title: NULLs and Three-Valued Logic
lessons.body:
Some cells hold no value at all. That is **NULL**, and it means `unknown` or `not recorded` — not zero, and not an empty string. In our data, unresolved tickets have NULL in `resolved_minutes`: nobody has measured them yet.

NULL breaks the usual rules because SQL uses **three-valued logic**: a comparison is `TRUE`, `FALSE`, or `UNKNOWN`. Any comparison with NULL is `UNKNOWN`, so `resolved_minutes = NULL` is never true, and `resolved_minutes != NULL` is never true either. A `WHERE` keeps a row only when its condition is `TRUE`, so both forms return nothing at all.

```sql
SELECT subject FROM tickets WHERE resolved_minutes = NULL;  -- always no rows
```

To test for NULL, use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`:

```sql
SELECT subject FROM tickets WHERE resolved_minutes IS NULL;
```

To substitute a fallback when a cell is NULL, use `COALESCE`, which returns its first non-NULL argument:

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(resolved_minutes, 0) FROM tickets;
```

The distinction also shows up in aggregates. `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is **not** NULL. On `tickets`, `COUNT(*)` is 10 while `COUNT(resolved_minutes)` is 5 — only five tickets have a recorded resolution time.

exercises.prompt: What does `SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE resolved_minutes = NULL;` return?
options: No rows, because a comparison with NULL is never true
All the tickets whose resolved_minutes is empty
Every ticket, because NULL matches everything
An error, because = cannot be used with a number
exercises.explain: Comparing anything to NULL yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so WHERE keeps no rows. You would use IS NULL instead.
exercises.hint: In SQL, NULL is unknown - it is not equal even to another NULL.

exercises.prompt: Which operator tests whether a column is NULL? (two words, for example 'IS ...')
exercises.hint: You cannot use = ; there is a dedicated two-word test.
exercises.explain: `col IS NULL` is true only when the cell is empty; `col IS NOT NULL` is the opposite.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets are there in total? Show just the count of rows.
exercises.hint: COUNT with a star inside the parentheses counts rows, NULLs and all.
exercises.explain: COUNT(*) counts every row, so it returns 10.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets actually have a resolution time recorded? Show just that count.
exercises.hint: COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values.
exercises.explain: Ten tickets exist, but only five hold a resolved_minutes value, so COUNT(resolved_minutes) is 5 - the same gap NULLs create.

lessons.title: Aggregates
lessons.body:
Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a single result row. There are five here:

| function | what it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `COUNT(*)` | number of rows |
| `COUNT(col)` | rows where col is not NULL |
| `SUM(col)` | total of a numeric column |
| `AVG(col)` | mean of a numeric column |
| `MIN(col)` / `MAX(col)` | smallest / largest value |

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets;
SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders;
SELECT AVG(resolved_minutes) FROM tickets;
SELECT MIN(total), MAX(total) FROM orders;
```

Every aggregate except `COUNT(*)` **ignores NULLs**. That is why `AVG(resolved_minutes)` divides by 5 (the recorded values), not by 10. The result of an aggregate query is always **one row**, and in this engine the column is named after the function exactly as written: `COUNT(*)`, `AVG(resolved_minutes)`, `MIN(total)`.

Aggregates respect `WHERE`, because they only see the rows that survive the filter:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open';
```

In full SQL you would summarise each group with `GROUP BY` — for example, one count per `status` — and then filter those groups with `HAVING`. This in-browser engine does not support `GROUP BY`, so every aggregate here describes the whole filtered table at once.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets are still Open? Show just the count.
exercises.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open'
exercises.hint: COUNT(*) counts the rows that survive the WHERE filter.
exercises.explain: Tickets 1, 4 and 9 are Open, so the count is 3.

exercises.prompt: What is the total value of all orders combined? Show just the sum.
exercises.hint: SUM adds the whole column together.

exercises.prompt: What is the average resolution time, in minutes, across the tickets that have one? Show just the average.
exercises.hint: AVG ignores the NULL cells, so it divides by the number of recorded values.
exercises.explain: 95+320+45+180+60 = 700 across 5 tickets, so the average is 140.

exercises.prompt: Which clause groups rows so that an aggregate is computed per group - for example, one ticket count for each status?
options: GROUP BY
ORDER BY
WHERE
LIMIT
exercises.explain: GROUP BY splits rows into groups before aggregating, and HAVING then filters those groups. This engine does not support GROUP BY, so here aggregates cover the whole filtered table.
exercises.hint: Its name says exactly what it does to rows.

lessons.title: Joining Tables
lessons.body:
Data is split across tables so nothing is stored twice. A ticket never repeats the customer's name; it stores `customer_id`, a number that points at a row in `customers`. That pointer is a **foreign key**, and a `JOIN` follows it:

```sql
SELECT tickets.subject, customers.name
FROM tickets
JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id;
```

Read it as: for each ticket row, find the customer row whose `id` equals the ticket's `customer_id`, then stitch the two into one output row. The `ON` clause is the matching rule; get it wrong and you get nonsense or no rows at all.

Tickets also carry `agent_id`, pointing at `agents`, so the same pattern answers who is handling what:

```sql
SELECT tickets.subject, agents.name
FROM tickets
JOIN agents ON tickets.agent_id = agents.id;
```

Two details matter. First, **qualify ambiguous columns**: both tables have an `id`, so write `tickets.id` or `customers.id` to say which you mean. Second, the result uses **bare column names** — `subject`, `name` — even though you typed `customers.name`. You can filter a joined table as freely as a base one:

```sql
SELECT tickets.subject FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.plan = 'Enterprise';
```

exercises.prompt: An order row has `customer_id = 5`. What does the 5 refer to?
options: The row in the customers table whose id is 5
The customer's fifth order
The agent who handled the order
A count of five customers
exercises.explain: customer_id is a foreign key: it points at customers.id, so it matches exactly one customer row.
exercises.hint: The number points across to another table.

exercises.prompt: Show each ticket's subject next to the name of the customer who raised it.
exercises.solution: SELECT tickets.subject, customers.name FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.hint: JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.explain: Ten tickets, each stitched to the customer that raised it.

exercises.prompt: List the subject of every ticket raised by an Enterprise-plan customer.
exercises.starter: SELECT tickets.subject FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.solution: SELECT tickets.subject FROM tickets JOIN customers ON tickets.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.plan = 'Enterprise'
exercises.hint: After the join, add WHERE customers.plan = 'Enterprise'.
exercises.explain: Northwind Traders and Tailspin Toys are the Enterprise customers - four tickets between them.

exercises.prompt: Show the id of each EMEA customer's orders next to the customer's name.
exercises.starter: SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
exercises.solution: SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id WHERE customers.region = 'EMEA'
exercises.hint: Join on the foreign key, then filter WHERE customers.region = 'EMEA'.
exercises.explain: The EMEA customers are Northwind Traders (orders 1, 3, 10) and Tailspin Toys (order 6).

lessons.title: Subqueries, IN and EXISTS
lessons.body:
A **subquery** is a `SELECT` nested inside another query. It runs first, produces a value or a list, and feeds the outer query — usually through the `WHERE` clause.

The simplest use is with `IN`: the inner query builds a list of values, and `IN` tests membership:

```sql
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open');
```

The inner query returns the customer ids that have an Open ticket; the outer query keeps only those customers. `NOT IN` is the opposite, with one NULL warning: if the inner list contains a NULL, `NOT IN` can quietly match nothing, because comparing with NULL yields `UNKNOWN`.

`EXISTS` tests whether the subquery returns **any** row, rather than which values it holds:

```sql
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tickets WHERE tickets.customer_id = customers.id AND status = 'Open');
```

The key difference: `IN` compares against a list and must build the whole list, while `EXISTS` can stop at the first matching row, so it is often faster on large tables. `EXISTS` also lets the inner query refer to the outer table (`customers.id`), which `IN` cannot do. Both answer the same everyday question — which customers have an Open ticket — and both are the bread and butter of support analytics.

exercises.prompt: What is a subquery?
options: A SELECT nested inside another query, whose result feeds the outer query
A copy of a table stored in memory
A query that runs on a second database
Another name for a JOIN
exercises.explain: A subquery is a full SELECT used as an input to an outer query, most often inside WHERE.
exercises.hint: The name tells you it sits inside something else.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword tests whether a value appears in a list produced by a subquery?
exercises.hint: Two letters; it is the opposite of NOT plus itself.
exercises.explain: `WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)` keeps rows whose value matches any value the subquery returned.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best describes EXISTS compared with IN?
options: EXISTS stops as soon as it finds one matching row, and can refer to the outer table
EXISTS always returns the list of matching values
EXISTS only works on numbers, IN only on text
They are identical in every respect
exercises.explain: EXISTS is a yes/no test, so it can short-circuit at the first match and can be correlated with the outer query.
exercises.hint: One asks 'which values', the other asks 'is there any row at all'.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order for finding every customer who has at least one Open ticket, using IN.
items: Run the inner query: SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open'
The inner query produces a list of customer ids
The outer query scans the customers table
WHERE customers.id IN (...) keeps customers whose id is in that list
exercises.explain: The inner query runs first to build the id list; the outer query then keeps only customers whose id appears in it.
exercises.hint: The list has to exist before the outer filter can test membership.

lessons.title: CTEs and Window Functions
lessons.body:
Two features make complex SQL readable and powerful. A **common table expression** (CTE) names a query with `WITH` so you can reuse it and read the logic top to bottom:

```sql
WITH open_tickets AS (
  SELECT id, customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'Open'
)
SELECT customers.name, open_tickets.id
FROM open_tickets
JOIN customers ON customers.id = open_tickets.customer_id;
```

The `WITH` block runs first and behaves like a temporary named table for the rest of the query. Chains of CTEs replace deeply nested subqueries and are far easier to debug.

**Window functions** compute a value across a set of rows *without* collapsing them — unlike aggregates, every row survives. They use an `OVER (...)` clause to define the window:

| function | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ROW_NUMBER()` | 1, 2, 3 ... unique per row |
| `RANK()` | same number for ties, then skips |
| `LAG(col)` | the previous row's value |

```sql
SELECT subject, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY resolved_minutes DESC) AS place
FROM tickets;
```

`ROW_NUMBER` numbers every row; `RANK` gives tied rows the same number and leaves gaps; `LAG` looks back one row, handy for how much a total changed since the last order. A CTE can even be **recursive** — it references itself — which is how you walk a reporting hierarchy, such as tickets escalated through managers. These run in a full database; this in-browser engine covers the single-table and join queries you have already practised.

exercises.prompt: What does a `WITH ... AS (...)` block do?
options: Names a query so later parts can use it like a temporary table
Permanently creates a new table in the database
Deletes rows that match a condition
Sorts the final result
exercises.explain: A CTE is a named, temporary result used by the main query. It makes complex logic readable and reusable.
exercises.hint: It is a nickname for a query, not a new stored table.

exercises.prompt: Which keyword begins a common table expression?
exercises.hint: Four letters; think 'WITH something AS (...)'.
exercises.explain: A CTE starts with `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)`, then the main query refers to that name.

exercises.prompt: Which window function gives tied rows the same number and then leaves a gap in the sequence?
options: RANK()
ROW_NUMBER()
LAG()
COUNT()
exercises.explain: RANK shares a number between ties and skips the next values; ROW_NUMBER is always unique; LAG looks one row back.
exercises.hint: Two rows with the same value should end up with the same rank.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order for how a CTE query is evaluated.
items: The WITH clause defines the CTE and runs its query
The CTE's result is held as a temporary named table
The main SELECT reads from the CTE, joining it to real tables if needed
The final result is returned to you
exercises.explain: The CTE is computed first and treated as a named result; the main query then reads it like a table.
exercises.hint: You cannot read the name until the WITH block has produced it.
